value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: letters can be treated as petitions, and M. C. Mehta vs. Union of India widened Articles 21 and 32; PIL does not follow strict locus standi
reasoning: PIL in India deliberately relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi, so any public-spirited person may approach the court; statement 1 is false. Courts have treated letters and postcards as writ petitions (epistolary jurisdiction), so statement 2 is true. M. C. Mehta vs. Union of India (Oleum gas leak, 1986) laid down absolute liability and held that the Supreme Court can award compensation under Article 32 for violation of Article 21, so statement 3 is true.

value: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; NOTA does not apply to the Presidential election

The vote is by secret ballot and no party whip binds electors, so statement 2 is true. NOTA is meant for direct elections and does not apply to the indirect election of the President (the Supreme Court excluded it from indirect elections in 2018), so statement 3 is false.

value: Only statement 2 is correct: residuary powers lie with the States in the US but with the Union in India
reasoning: Indian States did not exist independently before the federation and did not create it by agreement, so the Constitution has no US-style safeguards for State rights; statement 1 is false. In the US residuary powers stay with the States, while Article 248 gives them to the Union in India, so statement 2 is true. India borrowed the Union's residuary power from the Canadian Constitution, not the Irish one, so statement 3 is false.

value: Both statements are correct: four priority areas of work, and all assets go into the Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack

All assets created are aggregated into the Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack. This is recent current affairs, so the runner-up is A (1 only), which would win only if the infrastructure stack provision were described differently in the Act.

value: Both statements are correct: Article 20(1) bars ex post facto criminal laws
reasoning: Article 20(1) says no person shall be convicted except for breaking a law in force when the act was done, nor given a greater penalty than that law allowed, which is a bar on ex post facto laws; statement 1 is true. So a legislature cannot make a criminal law retrospective to convict or punish, which is what statement 2 says. Runner-up A (1 only): it would win if the examiner reads statement 2 strictly, since the bar covers only conviction and penalty and procedural criminal law can still be retrospective.
